_note: AUTHORITATIVE RULE CONTENT. Do not add, remove or alter nodes, clocks, section references or authorities. If something is missing, stop and ask.

intake.q: What do you want to know?

nodes.title: Check which government this belongs to
nodes.summary: The central portal will not accept state matters, and it does not refund the fee.
nodes.body: rtionline.gov.in accepts applications only for ministries, departments and other public authorities of the Central Government. Its own homepage carries a warning in red that applications filed there for state government bodies, including the Government of NCT of Delhi, will be returned and the amount will not be refunded. Most everyday problems, such as municipal work, state police, state schools, land records and state pensions, are state matters. If yours is one of those, you need your state's own RTI portal, or you file on paper to the state public authority.

warnings.text: This is a state government matter. If you file it on the central portal the application is returned and your fee is not refunded. We will still draft it for you to file with your state or by post.
You are not sure which government this belongs to. Getting it wrong costs you the fee with no refund, so it is worth checking before you pay.

nodes.title: This may be a grievance rather than an RTI
nodes.summary: RTI gets you records. It cannot make anyone act.
nodes.body: The Right to Information Act gives you access to information held by a public authority. It does not give you the power to make an official do something, and a request phrased as a demand for action is likely to be refused. If you want something fixed, a grievance to CPGRAMS is the right route. You can do both, and it often helps: an RTI asking what has been done so far frequently moves a file that a grievance alone did not.

nodes.title: Find the right public authority and its officer
nodes.summary: Addressing the wrong officer is the most common way applications die.
nodes.body: Every public authority appoints a Central Public Information Officer, or a State PIO for state bodies. Your application goes to that officer. On the central portal, applications reach the Nodal Officer of the ministry or department, who transmits them to the CPIO. If you address the wrong authority, the officer receiving it should transfer it to the correct one within five days under Section 6(3), but that transfer is not guaranteed and it costs you time. The government maintains a directory of PIOs and Appellate Authorities on its RTI Portal Gateway, which is a separate website from the one where you file.

warnings.text: The directory of officers is on rti.gov.in. The place you file is rtionline.gov.in. They are different sites and neither tells you clearly that you need both.

nodes.sourceLabel: RTI Act 2005, sections 5 and 6(3); RTI Portal Gateway

nodes.title: Write it so it cannot be refused
nodes.summary: Ask for records, not for reasons.
nodes.body: The Act covers information held in material form: records, documents, memos, file notings, orders, logbooks, contracts and reports. It does not cover opinions, explanations or answers to questions. This is why 'why has my pension not been released' is refusable and 'provide a copy of the file notings on application number X, the current stage of processing, and the name and designation of the officer holding the file' is not. You are also not required to give any reason for wanting the information, and you should not be asked for one. Keep each application to one subject and one public authority. Unrelated questions in a single application get split, transferred and half answered.

warnings.text: The application text is limited to 3,000 characters. Anything longer has to go in as an attachment.
Only these characters are accepted in the request text: A to Z, a to z, 0 to 9, and , . - _ ( ) / @ : & ? \ % — anything else will break the form.

nodes.sourceLabel: RTI Act 2005, sections 2(f), 2(i), 2(j) and 6(2); RTI Online guidelines

nodes.title: Check it before you pay
nodes.summary: Six things that get applications rejected, all of them avoidable.
nodes.body: Every one of these has caused applications to be returned or refused. The portal checks none of them for you before it takes your money.

warnings.text: Do not attach your Aadhaar, PAN or any other identity document. Section 6(2) does not require identity proof. The only identity document the portal asks for is a BPL certificate, and only if you are claiming free filing.
Any attachment must be a single PDF under 1 MB, and the filename must contain no spaces.
Ask for the information in electronic form. If you ask for paper copies you will be charged per page for anything beyond the first set.

nodes.sourceLabel: RTI Online guidelines; RTI Act 2005, section 6(2); RTI Rules 2012

nodes.title: File it on the central portal and pay the fee
nodes.summary: Ten rupees, or free if your household is below the poverty line.
nodes.body: The application fee is ten rupees, prescribed under the RTI Rules 2012, and there is no fee at all for applicants below the poverty line, though you must attach the certificate issued by the appropriate government. Payment on the portal goes through a payment gateway that opens in a separate tab. Once the application is submitted you receive a unique registration number, in a format such as DOPTR/E/2026/00000, which you will need for tracking and for any appeal.

warnings.text: If the payment goes through but no registration number appears, wait 24 to 48 working hours. Do not try to pay again. If it still has not appeared, email the helpdesk with the transaction details.
You are filing free as a BPL applicant, so remember to attach the certificate. Without it the application will not be accepted.

nodes.title: File it with your state
nodes.summary: The same law, a different counter.
nodes.body: The Right to Information Act applies to state public authorities in exactly the same way. Only the destination changes. Most states run their own online RTI portal. Where a state does not, or where the portal is unavailable, an application on plain paper delivered or posted to the State Public Information Officer is equally valid. There is no prescribed form. The fee is ten rupees, and there is no fee if you hold a BPL certificate.

warnings.text: The central portal will not take this. The law still will.
Send it by registered post if you file on paper. The thirty day clock runs from the date the authority receives it, so you need proof of that date.
An application handed to an Assistant Public Information Officer is valid. Five days are added to the reply period under the proviso to section 7(1).

nodes.sourceLabel: RTI Act 2005 sections 6(1) and 7(1); RTI Rules 2012

nodes.title: If it went to the wrong office
nodes.summary: They have five days to send it to the right one.
nodes.body: If the public authority that receives your application does not hold the information, Section 6(3) requires it to transfer the application to the authority that does, and to inform you, within five days. Time for the reply then runs from the date the correct authority receives it, which is why a transfer effectively adds to your wait.

clock.label: Transfer to the correct authority
clock.consequence: the clock restarts from the date the correct authority receives it

nodes.title: Wait for the reply
nodes.summary: Thirty days. Forty eight hours if life or liberty is involved.
nodes.body: The Public Information Officer must provide the information, or reject the request with reasons, within thirty days of receiving it. Where the request concerns the life or liberty of a person, the period is forty eight hours. If the application was filed through an Assistant PIO, five days are added. If the information relates to a third party, the authority must give that party notice and the period extends to forty days.

clock.label: Reply due
clock.consequence: silence becomes a deemed refusal and you may appeal

clockOverrides.label: Reply due, life or liberty
clockOverrides.consequence: silence becomes a deemed refusal and you may appeal

warnings.text: This concerns life or liberty, so the officer has forty eight hours, not thirty days. Say so clearly in the application, because otherwise it will be treated as an ordinary request.
If the authority asks for additional fees to cover the cost of providing the information, the clock stops until you pay. That intimation appears on the portal and by email.

nodes.title: They did not reply, so in law they refused
nodes.summary: You can appeal now. You do not need a rejection letter.
nodes.body: Where the Public Information Officer fails to give a decision within the time specified, the officer is deemed to have refused the request under Section 7(2). This is the single most useful thing most applicants never learn. Silence is not the end of the matter. It is a refusal, it starts your right of appeal, and you do not need any letter from the department to act on it.

nodes.title: File the First Appeal
nodes.summary: Free. Thirty days to file. They have up to forty five days to decide.
nodes.body: A First Appeal goes to an officer senior in rank to the Public Information Officer, called the First Appellate Authority, within the same public authority. You may appeal if you received no reply, if the reply was incomplete or misleading, or if the information was refused. No fee is payable for a first appeal. The appeal must normally be filed within thirty days of the decision or of the date the reply was due, though the Appellate Authority may admit a late appeal if satisfied there was sufficient cause. The Authority must dispose of the appeal within thirty days, extendable to a maximum of forty five days with reasons recorded in writing.

clock.label: Deadline to file the First Appeal
clock.consequence: you may still apply, but you will need to show sufficient cause for the delay

warnings.text: There is no fee for a first appeal. Anyone asking you to pay for one is wrong.
Quote the registration number of the original application. Without it the appeal cannot be linked to your request.

nodes.title: File the Second Appeal to the Information Commission
nodes.summary: Ninety days. The Commission can penalise the officer personally.
nodes.body: If the First Appellate Authority refuses, or does not decide, you may appeal to the Central Information Commission, or the State Information Commission for state bodies. A second appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date the decision should have been made or was actually received, and the Commission may admit a later appeal for sufficient cause. A second appeal filed without a first appeal is liable to be returned. The Central Information Commission has integrated its second appeal filing with the RTI Online portal, so entering the First Appeal registration number, the email address and the filing date pulls the earlier details across automatically.

clock.label: Deadline to file the Second Appeal
clock.consequence: you may still apply, but you will need to show sufficient cause for the delay

warnings.text: You cannot skip the First Appeal. A second appeal filed without one is liable to be returned.

nodes.sourceLabel: RTI Act 2005, section 19(3); RTI Online portal notice on CIC integration

nodes.title: Complain about the officer's conduct
nodes.summary: A different route, with no time limit at all.
nodes.body: An appeal challenges the decision. A complaint under Section 18 challenges the conduct of the officer: refusing to accept your application, demanding a reason for wanting the information, giving deliberately misleading information, or charging an unreasonable fee. It goes directly to the Information Commission and, unlike an appeal, it carries no time limit. The Commission can impose a penalty on the officer personally through either route.

warnings.text: A complaint and an appeal do different jobs. Use a complaint when the officer behaved improperly, and an appeal when you disagree with the decision.

nodes.sourceLabel: RTI Act 2005, section 18; RTI Online process flowchart

checks.label: Correct government
checks.fail: This is a state matter, so the central portal will return it. Your state route is set out at the filing step.
checks.fix: Nothing to fix if the records are held by a state body. Continue and file with your state.

checks.label: Under 3,000 characters
checks.fail: Longer text has to go in as a PDF attachment instead.
checks.fix: Shorten the text, or move the detail into a PDF attachment under 1 MB.

checks.label: Accepted characters only
checks.fail: The form accepts only A-Z a-z 0-9 and , . - _ ( ) / @ : & ? \ % — remove anything else.
checks.fix: Remove the flagged characters. Rupee signs, curly quotes and em dashes are the usual culprits.

checks.label: One subject, one authority
checks.fail: Unrelated questions in one application get transferred and half answered.
checks.fix: Split this into separate applications. We can do that for you.

checks.label: Asks for records, not reasons
checks.fail: The Act covers information held in material form. Questions and requests for explanations can be refused.
checks.fix: Ask for the document instead of the reason. For example, 'provide a copy of the file notings' rather than 'why was this delayed'.

checks.label: No identity documents attached
checks.fail: Section 6(2) does not require identity proof. Do not upload Aadhaar or PAN.
checks.fix: Remove the attachment. You do not need to prove who you are to make an RTI request.

checks.label: PDF under 1 MB, no spaces in the filename
checks.fix: Save as a single PDF under 1 MB and rename it without spaces.

checks.label: BPL certificate attached
checks.fail: Free filing requires the certificate issued by the appropriate government.
checks.fix: Attach the BPL certificate issued by your state government, or switch to paid filing at the ten rupee fee.
